description: We are a student engineering and astrophysics team combining ESP32-S3 hardware, optical photometry sensors, Python (Streamlit), and Random Forest Machine Learning to simulate how space telescopes detect exoplanets and predict their orbits in real time. Join us if you love hands-on space tech, live mission-control dashboards, and applying AI to cosmic discovery. We have our core hardware and coding stack covered, and we value skills in NASA dataset integration, UI polish, and presentation design!
summary:
To address the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge, our team developed the AI Powered Exoplanet Hunter, an interactive hardware-and-software training simulator. We engineered a physical exoplanet transit rig using an ESP32-S3 microcontroller and an optical photometer, paired with a live Python Streamlit Mission Control dashboard.

Our project trains junior astronauts by placing them directly in the seat of a Mission Director. Trainees must monitor a live optical telemetry stream, calibrate detection thresholds to filter out sensor noise, and analyze real-time light curves to confirm planetary dips. As transits occur, the software calculates the planet-to-star radius ratio and evaluates an illustrative Habitable Zone. Finally, trainees use our integrated, pre-trained Random Forest Machine Learning model to forecast the exact timing of future orbital transits.

This trainer is important because it transforms abstract astrophysics and data science into a hands-on, accessible experience. By bridging physical hardware with live AI evaluation, it provides an authentic simulation of how real NASA missions like Kepler and TESS hunt for life beyond Earth, actively inspiring the next generation of space explorers.
details:
1. What it does and how it works

The AI Powered Exoplanet Hunter is an end-to-end mission simulator that bridges physical hardware with live data science. It works in two parts:

  • The Hardware Observatory: A motorized tabletop rig simulates a planetary orbit, moving a physical exoplanet model across a bright light source (the star). An ESP32-S3 microcontroller reads light intensity using a Light-Dependent Resistor (LDR) housed inside a light-shielding telescope tube, streaming telemetry via USB serial at 115,200 baud.
  • The Mission Control Dashboard: A single-page Python Streamlit application (live_dashboard_nasa_plus.py) reads this live telemetry. It plots a 3-trace light curve, uses a rule-based algorithm to verify transit dips, calculates the planet-to-star radius ratio ($R_p / R_*$), and feeds the observed transit intervals into a pre-trained Scikit-Learn Random Forest Regressor to predict the exact timing of the next orbit.

2. Tools, Coding Languages, and Hardware Used

  • Hardware: ESP32-S3 microcontroller, optical LDR (photoresistor) sensor, DC motorized transit platform, and breadboard circuitry.
  • Languages: Python (for the dashboard, data analysis, and AI pipeline) and C++ (Arduino IDE for the ESP32 sensor firmware).
  • Software & Libraries: Streamlit (UI and live dashboard), Scikit-Learn (Random Forest ML model), Pandas & NumPy (data structuring and rolling median filters), Matplotlib (offline light curve analysis), and Joblib (model serialization).

3. How the project is creative and factors our team considered

Most software projects rely purely on pre-existing static datasets. Our project is creative because it generates its own physical data in real-time, forcing us to solve real-world engineering problems.

When building the detection algorithm, our team had to consider electrical sensor noise and ambient room light. To prevent false positives, we engineered a state-machine that requires 3 consecutive sub-threshold readings to officially log a transit. To ensure our AI wasn't just a "black box," we rigorously evaluated our Random Forest model using Leave-One-Recording-Out cross-validation across multiple experimental CSV runs, scoring its accuracy live using Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE).

4. Benefits and Intended Impact

As a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer, this project takes the highly abstract concepts of deep-space astrophysics (transit photometry, light curves, and orbital mechanics) and turns them into a gamified, tactile experience.

The primary benefit is hands-on education: users actively calibrate optical thresholds, watch physical shadows translate into digital data dips, and see how machine learning predicts future cosmic events. The intended impact is to demystify how real space telescopes like Kepler, TESS, and JWST operate, inspiring students by proving that with accessible microcontrollers and Python, anyone can build their own deep-space observatory.
